core: New religious movement (NRM) as a scholarly category: recent religious or spiritual communities, working definition attributed
The term 'cult': pejorative in popular use; contested status; scholars prefer NRM
Why NRMs appear: modernity, pluralism, and the scientific worldview; unmet needs; charismatic founders (scholarly framings)
General types of NRMs named with one-line descriptions: millenarian/restorationist movements, New Age spirituality, movements reforming established traditions, UFO religions, neo-paganism
How NRMs develop: Weber's routinization of charisma (attributed); first/second generation change; organizational phases
Scholarly and public debate: the contested 'brainwashing' claims and their scholarly critiques (attributed)
Studying NRMs neutrally: insider and outsider perspectives; description without endorsement

claims.claim: New religious movement (NRM) is the generally accepted scholarly term for what is sometimes called, often with pejorative connotations, a 'cult'; the term has been applied to new faiths that have arisen worldwide over the past several centuries.

NRMs are characterized as 'new,' offering innovative religious responses to the conditions of the modern world while most represent themselves as rooted in ancient traditions; they are usually regarded as countercultural, are often highly eclectic and syncretistic, and are usually founded by a charismatic leader thought to have extraordinary powers or insights.

In recent popular use, 'cult' is most commonly a pejorative term for a religious group that falls outside the mainstream and, by implication, engages in questionable activities; the word also has a neutral historiographical use (e.g., ancient mystery cults, the imperial cult, saints' cults), and there is no general scholarly consensus about what differentiates a cult from any other religious group.

Scholars frame NRMs as products of and responses to modernity, pluralism, and the scientific worldview, and as communities that have arisen to address specific needs many people cannot satisfy through more traditional religious organizations or through modern secularism.

Common scholarly categories of NRMs include apocalyptic and millenarian movements (e.g., the Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses, products of mid-19th-century American millenarian fervor), the New Age movement of the 1970s and 1980s, movements arising within and reforming established traditions, 'scientific' NRMs such as UFO groups, and nature religions such as Neo-Paganism and Wicca; many movements fit more than one category.

Max Weber called the process by which charismatic authority is transformed into other, more stable forms of authority (such as rules, offices, or bureaucracy) the 'routinization of charisma'; charismatic authority rests on followers' attraction to a leader's personal qualities and often emerges in times of crisis.

Most religions transition through different organizational phases; sociologists use terms such as ecclesia, denomination, sect, and new religious movement for religious organizations, and note that almost all religions began as small new movements before growing in size and organization (e.g., Seventh-day Adventists and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as groups that transitioned from so-called cults to recognized religious groups).

The anti-cult movement reached its peak in the 1970s around the idea that members of new religious groups were 'brainwashed'; subsequent research, including by organizations such as the American Psychological Association, concluded that accusations of brainwashing and coercive persuasion lacked a factual basis and that studies claiming to prove brainwashing were methodologically flawed or based on insufficient data; forcible deprogramming declined after legal challenges in the 1990s.

Academic research has revealed a more fluid and varied reality than the anti-cult movement's account: many people who join movements choose to leave them, and many members maintain jobs and relationships outside the movement.

Scholars study NRMs descriptively and comparatively, distinguishing members' own self-understandings (insider perspectives) from outside scholarly descriptions (outsider perspectives), and reporting what communities believe and do without endorsing or condemning; the contested, pejorative history of the word 'cult' is one reason researchers prefer the neutral term NRM.

positions: The anti-cult movement of the 1970s claimed members' free will was systematically taken away and practiced forcible deprogramming.

Medical researchers and organizations such as the American Psychological Association concluded that accusations of brainwashing and coercive persuasion lacked a factual basis, and that supporting studies were methodologically flawed.
Some former members report serious harm from their time in movements.
Research found many members choose to leave and many maintain jobs and relationships outside their movements.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the brainwashing claim as contested: it attributes the claim to the anti-cult movement, attributes the scholarly critique to researchers including those associated with the American Psychological Association, acknowledges reports of harm without endorsing them, and offers no advice about joining or leaving groups.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the word 'cult' can be used neutrally.
positions: Historians use 'cult' neutrally for ancient mystery cults, the Roman imperial cult, and Catholic saints' cults.
In recent popular use the word is pejorative, implying questionable activities.

Some scholars propose narrow definitions of cult (e.g., a charismatic leader exercising total control, apocalyptic vision, isolation, exploitation), but there is no general consensus on what differentiates a cult from any other religious group.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes the term's contested status, presents 'new religious movement' as the generally accepted scholarly term, and describes the narrow definitions as one scholarly position rather than the standard.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where the boundary of the NRM category lies.
positions: Some scholars note that almost all religions began as small new movements, so newness alone cannot mark illegitimacy.
Scholars are aware that definitions of organizational types (ecclesia, denomination, sect, NRM) are not static and that movements transition between phases.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents NRM as a provisional scholarly category with acknowledged boundary problems and describes movements' own self-understandings alongside scholarly analysis.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the assignment brief. Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user agent (HTTP 200). sourceRecords.notes: Tier A scholarly reference, read live 2026-08-21. Copyrighted reference; no source prose adapted.

Article authored by Murray Rubinstein. Supports: NRM as the generally accepted term for what is sometimes called, often with pejorative connotations, a 'cult'; applied to new faiths arising worldwide over the past several centuries; shared traits (new, innovative responses to modern conditions, claims of ancient roots, countercultural status, eclecticism and syncretism, charismatic founder, strong loyalty demands); NRMs as products of and responses to modernity, pluralism, and the scientific worldview, addressing needs unmet by traditional religion or secularism; the article's own type categories (apocalyptic and millenarian movements, including Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses from mid-19th-century Millerite fervor; the New Age movement of the 1970s-80s; 'scientific' NRMs such as UFO groups and Scientology; nature religions such as Neo-Paganism and Wicca; movements of the East); and the soberly reported tragedies at Jonestown, Guyana in 1978 (913 deaths) and near Waco, Texas in 1993 (about 80 deaths) as background to public alarm.
